pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 21. Errors today: 350. Foam incidents: 3.*

Three days before the Fair, the machine reached link thirty-four. The class held its breath while the air in Alvarado Fix-It grew thick, resembling a balloon waiting to pop. Tobias stood at the control panel with his bow tie perfectly straight, his hands trembling slightly on the levers. He had added his own idea: a foam-making tube to signal the finish. It was elegant. It was logical. It was, as it turned out, a catastrophic oversight.

He pressed the lever for the final click.

Nothing happened.

He pressed it again, and a low, wet hiss came from the top of the machine. A single drop of white foam landed on the marble ramp, followed quickly by another, then a steady stream. The tube, which should have released a small puff, began to gurgle as the pressure gauge spun past red into a color that did not exist on the scale.

"Stop," Tobias said, his voice very small.

It did not stop.

The foam hit the first domino, then the second, then the third. They were not falling. They were floating.
pages.image: A tall, neat boy with dark hair and glasses stands frozen before a complex Rube Goldberg machine, his hands on a lever, while a thick stream of white foam erupts from a tube and washes over the initial wooden blocks in a cluttered workshop.

pages.text:
The foam did not stop. It expanded, spreading and climbing until, within thirty seconds, the floor of Alvarado Fix-It was gone. The toasters were buried, the workbench became a white plateau, and the parrot perched on a high shelf was covered in suds, its feathers glistening.

Tobias stood on a stool, waist-deep in the white sludge. His bow tie, once crisp and dark, was now a soggy, pale ribbon hanging around his neck, while his glasses fogged over. He looked at the foam, then at the class, and his face went the color of the foam itself.

"It was my fault," he said. The words came out flat and final. "The pressure valve. I calculated it wrong. I am sorry. I want to go home."

He did not move. He could not move. The foam was warm and smelled faintly of soap and regret. Bea looked at him, then at the mess, then back at him. The parrot blinked.

"Not yet," it said. Its voice was very small, muffled by a layer of suds.
pages.image: A boy with pale skin and glasses stands waist-deep in thick white foam in a cluttered workshop, his bow tie soaking wet and limp, looking distressed, while a small parrot covered in foam blinks from a high shelf in the background.

pages.text:
I examined the foam, then the machine, which had become a sculptural piece of white art, then Tobias, who was vibrating with the urge to apologize again. My internal protocols demanded I report the error rate, suggest a cleanup schedule, and be perfect.

I swallowed the demand.

"That was the best thing I have ever seen," I said.

The room went silent, save for the drip of foam.

Tobias looked up. "It is a disaster."

"Yes," I said. "It is a disaster. And it is beautiful. And it was your idea." I looked at Bea, then at the rest of them. My chest light flickered in a warm, irregular pulse. I did not have a word for the feeling yet. It felt like the foam: soft and unplanned.

I laughed, a short, dry sound like a servo releasing tension. Bea looked at me, then at the foam, and then she laughed. One by one, the rest of the class joined in. It was not a mean laugh, but a loud, happy, bubbling one.
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes and a glowing chest light stands in a workshop filled with white foam, looking at a boy with glasses, while a group of children in the background smile and laugh, the air bright and chaotic.

pages.text:
The dripping slowed to a quiet rhythm as we sat on the high stools, picking suds from our hair. Tobias wiped his bow tie with a rag, then gave up on it entirely, looking at Bea with a strange, vulnerable expression.

"Can I go in the journal?" he asked.

Bea stopped picking at her bun. She looked at him for a long time. "Which one?"

"The one with the failures. The one with what I learned." He took off his glasses and cleaned them on his shirt, his hands trembling slightly. "I have spent my whole life making sure I was not wrong in front of people. It is very tiring. I would like to be wrong out loud. Just once. In the record."

Bea opened her battered notebook and flipped to the end. Her pencil moved across the page with the confidence of someone who had done this many times before.

"Entry 217," she said. "Tobias Pym. What I learned: being wrong out loud isn't the end of the world; it's the end of hiding."

She handed him the page. He looked at it. He did not say thank you. He just nodded, and for the first time, his shoulders dropped.
pages.image: A boy with dark hair and glasses looks down at a small open notebook held by a short girl with curly hair and a yellow raincoat, both sitting on wooden stools in a workshop, the boy's expression relieved and quiet, the girl's focused and kind.

pages.text:
That night I added one more line to my log. *Confession: I am afraid that I will not be able to make it work in time. This is a new reading and I do not like it. I think it is what other people call worry.*

I stared at the words in the dark. They were not an error, but a fact. I switched off the main light and sat in the quiet. My chest light flickered, slow and soft, like a video game loading a new level.

From the cage on the table, Gerald stirred. He climbed onto his wheel and, surprisingly, did not fall off. He ran and ran, the wheel humming softly in the silence. I watched him until the first gray light of dawn touched the window. He stayed on the wheel. I did not know why, and I did not need to know. I just watched.
pages.image: A small silver-white robot sits in a dark, narrow cupboard, his chest light glowing softly, watching a fawn-and-white hamster run steadily on a wheel in a small cage, the scene quiet and still, with a faint glow from the robot's light.
